details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: How should energy, raw materials, and direct labour hours be combined into the single resource denominator — and what are their relative weights (e.g. cost-based: 1 kWh ≈ £0.15, 1 kg material ≈ £2.00, 1 labour-hour ≈ £18)? Without explicit weights the optimiser cannot evaluate the ratio and may collapse all resource cost to whichever component has the largest raw numeric value.
flags.resolution: Apply cost-normalised weights derived from the site's most recent standard cost sheet; if unavailable, use equal unit-cost weights (1:1:1) and flag the assumption for manager review before the schedule is executed.

flags.question: Is the fatigue limit of 0.4 a continuous intra-shift ceiling (fatigue index must never exceed 0.4 at any moment during the shift) or an end-of-shift snapshot constraint (index ≤ 0.4 only at shift close)? The optimiser can legally front-load heavy tasks and briefly spike fatigue above 0.4 under the snapshot interpretation, which likely violates the manager's safety intent.
flags.resolution: Treat the 0.4 limit as a continuous ceiling enforced at every re-optimisation interval (default: every 15 minutes); any plan candidate that projects a fatigue exceedance at any future checkpoint within the shift is rejected.

flags.field: resource_efficiency — absence of minimum throughput floor
flags.question: Is there a minimum delivered-value target (production quota) for the shift — for example, at least 800 units or £12 000 of output — below which the shift is considered a failure regardless of efficiency ratio? Without a floor the optimiser can legally maximise the value/resource ratio by producing a single high-margin item and idling, which would not meet actual production commitments.
flags.resolution: Apply a minimum throughput floor equal to 90 % of the rolling 30-shift average delivered value for this shift type; if historical data are unavailable, set the floor to the contractual customer-order volume for the shift.

flags.question: Does the 80 dB(A) limit apply as a continuous instantaneous ceiling (no reading may exceed 80 dB(A) at any moment) or as a time-averaged LAeq over the full shift per ISO 9612? Cyclic machines commonly generate peaks of 85–90 dB(A) that average below 80 dB(A); the choice determines which equipment-selection and sequencing options remain feasible.
flags.resolution: Enforce 80 dB(A) as the shift-level LAeq per ISO 9612, consistent with the assumption already stated in the contract, while additionally rejecting any plan that produces a predicted instantaneous peak above 90 dB(A) (EU Directive 2003/10/EC upper exposure action value).

flags.question: What is the planned duration of this shift (e.g. 8 h, 10 h, 12 h)? Shift length directly calibrates the fatigue-accumulation trajectory (a 0.4 fatigue index reached after 6 h implies a different work-intensity profile than after 10 h), the LAeq noise average, and whether intra-shift rolling re-optimisation windows are wide enough to be meaningful.
flags.resolution: Assume a standard 8-hour shift (480 minutes) with a 30-minute unpaid break excluded from fatigue and noise accumulation; flag the assumption in the generated schedule header so the manager can correct it before execution.

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: The contract schedule S1 was planned around a demand baseline of 52.0 UPH. A +20% surge to 62.4 UPH means the total unit obligation within the Phase 2 window increased proportionally, while the schedule's time allocation and resource pacing were sized for the original target. Actual throughput (40.7 UPH) is not only below the surged demand rate (62.4 UPH) but also below the original baseline, indicating that higher cycle pressure from the demand surge has created queuing and pacing inefficiencies rather than increased output. The resulting production deficit accumulates over time: each hour the system runs at 40.7 UPH against a 62.4 UPH obligation, a backlog of ~21.7 units compounds. This backlog pushes the projected completion timestamp past the contractual deadline, collapsing the DeadlineGap margin (currently 0.348, flagged as breached). The physics pathway is: demand surge → increased cycle dispatch rate → resource contention and pacing mismatch → throughput suppressed below even pre-surge levels → deadline slip accelerates nonlinearly as phase time elapses.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Immediately escalate to operations supervisor. Trigger a schedule replan with revised demand input (62.4 UPH) to recompute feasible completion time. Simultaneously evaluate short-term throughput levers: authorize controlled robot speed increase (monitor noise_db and energy_kwh headroom — both currently have margin), check operator availability to reduce workload redistribution lag, and assess whether any lower-priority batches in Phase 2 can be deferred to protect deadline-critical units. If replanning confirms the deadline is unrecoverable under current constraints, initiate customer/stakeholder notification protocol now rather than at phase end.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: r2 is operating at full speed (1.0), making it the dominant noise contributor. Noise scales approximately linearly with robot speed fraction; an 8% reduction in r2 speed should yield roughly a 5 dB decrease, bringing noise from 84.9 dB down to approximately 80.0 dB. This is the smallest single-parameter change that can address the noise violation.

FatigueIndex is the most severely violated constraint (0.6001 vs limit 0.4). Fatigue scales proportionally with cycle rate; the target multiplier is 1.15 × (0.4 / 0.6001) ≈ 0.767. Reducing to 0.77 brings fatigue to the boundary (≈0.401) with minimal throughput sacrifice. A value of 0.75 would add a small safety buffer if exact linearity cannot be guaranteed.

Increasing buffer time from 0.85 s to 1.0 s provides additional recovery windows between cycles, reducing peak physiological load on the human operator. This acts as a secondary lever for fatigue (complementing the cycle-rate reduction) and marginally reduces robot active-time share, offering a small ancillary noise and energy benefit. Adjust only if throughput target allows the additional idle time.

details.trigger: Autonomous replan failed; escalation to human manager

details.conflict: A 20% demand surge has made the current production schedule infeasible under active human-centric constraints. The proposed schedule violates two worker-protection limits simultaneously: FatigueIndex is 0.2001 above its ceiling (observed 0.6001 vs. limit 0.40), and occupational Noise exposure is 4.9 dB above its ceiling (observed 84.9 dB vs. limit 80.0 dB). No feasible schedule exists within current staffing levels and constraint boundaries. Human oversight is required before rescheduling can proceed. Both violations directly affect worker health and safety and cannot be resolved automatically by the CBPA optimizer without manager authorization.
options: Option 1 (Recommended): Distribute Load via Supplementary Shifts and Cross-Trained Workers
Option 2 (Moderate): Temporarily Raise FatigueIndex Ceiling to 0.50 with Mandatory Compensatory Rest Protocol
Option 3 (Last Resort): Relax Both FatigueIndex (0.55) and Noise (83.0 dB) with Engineering Controls and Occupational Health Oversight

details.reasoning_rationale: Three independent signals all converge on MACRO: (1) P(feasible)=0.00% leaves zero margin for incremental fixes — MICRO parameter tweaks of ±5% speed or ±10% cycle rate are arithmetically incapable of recovering feasibility from a complete failure; (2) FatigueIndex is violated at 100% probability, meaning the constraint is not merely stressed but structurally broken under the current schedule and a +20% demand surge — fatigue is a hard physiological/operational ceiling that cannot be patched by speed adjustments alone, and increasing throughput to meet the surge would worsen it further; (3) prior learning is unambiguous: across 6 identical prior situations, MESO (S2) was rejected every single time and MACRO (S3) was accepted every single time, providing a 100% empirical base rate for MACRO.
details.reasoning_key_insight: The FatigueIndex constraint is intrinsically incompatible with a +20% demand surge at current capacity configuration — full L1-L2 replanning is required to restructure rest cycles, robot/worker allocation, or throughput routing in a way that simultaneously satisfies fatigue limits and meets elevated demand. Prior experience eliminates any ambiguity: MESO has never succeeded in this scenario class.

experience_synthesis.insight: S2 is deterministically rejected for demand_surge due to hard constraint violations (Fatigue > 0.4 and Noise > 80dB) — no stochastic variation observed across all 6 trials, making this a reliable exclusion rule. S3 succeeds in 6/6 trials with satisfaction=True, but exhibits notable performance variability: throughput_uph ranges from 24.6 to 38.0 UPH and deadline_gap_pct from 41.5% to 58.9%. The bimodal clustering in metrics (low-throughput cluster ~24-26 UPH with ~58-59% deadline gap vs. high-throughput cluster ~37-38 UPH with ~42-44% deadline gap) suggests S3 outcomes depend on secondary contextual factors not captured in these records. Planners should prefer S3 unconditionally over S2 for demand_surge, but should anticipate and plan for throughput variance. Confidence is moderate-high given 100% policy consistency but tempered by the small sample (n=6) and unresolved source of performance bimodality.
